title: Sizing London's market for electric cargo bikes
prompt: Tandrel, a European maker of electric cargo bikes, is thinking about opening a sales and service centre in London aimed at delivery businesses. Before it decides, it wants to know how big the opportunity is. Estimate the yearly market, in pounds, for new electric cargo bikes bought by delivery businesses in London, and tell the client whether it is big enough.

facts.answer: Tandrel makes electric cargo bikes and sells them in several European cities. It would open a London sales and service centre only if it could expect at least £2 million of bike sales a year there.

New electric cargo bikes bought each year by businesses that deliver goods in Greater London, valued at the price paid. Count a leased bike once, at its purchase price. Leave out servicing, spare batteries, insurance and riders' pay.

Three groups: parcel carriers, grocery and meal-kit delivery firms, and local businesses that deliver their own goods, such as pharmacies, florists and print shops. A table of deliveries by segment is available.
Leave them out. Takeaway riders mostly use their own ordinary bikes or e-bikes, not cargo bikes, and the delivery businesses do not buy them.
Estimate next year's market, starting from the bikes working in London today.
Assume a cargo bike in daily delivery use lasts about 4 years before it is replaced.
Assume the number of electric cargo bikes working for London delivery businesses grows by 25% next year, as more businesses swap vans for bikes in central areas.
Assume an average price of £6,000 per bike, including the cargo box and battery, after fleet discounts.
Once its centre is running, Tandrel expects to win about 20% of the market, similar to its share in other cities where it has a service centre.
Ignore them. Delivery businesses almost always buy new bikes so that they get the warranty and servicing.

key_buckets: Define the market: new bikes bought per year, in pounds, by delivery businesses in London
Segment the users: parcel carriers, grocery and meal kits, local businesses
Working fleet per segment: deliveries made by bike divided by deliveries per bike per day
Yearly purchases: replacing worn-out bikes plus growth of the fleet
Value and the client's question: bikes times price, then Tandrel's share against its £2 million bar
good_signs: Separates the number of bikes in use (the fleet) from the number bought each year
Segments by type of delivery business rather than starting from London's population
States each assumption clearly and rounds to keep the maths simple
Sense-checks the result and names the assumption that matters most
red_flags: Treats the whole fleet as if it were bought every year
Counts takeaway riders' own bikes or e-bikes
Gives a market size without answering whether it is big enough for the client

exhibits.title: Deliveries in London per day, by segment (case assumptions)
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask how many deliveries each segment makes, how many are made by cargo bike, and how many deliveries one bike makes in a day.
exhibits.insight: The working fleet is about 5,000 bikes: 1,500 for parcels, 1,500 for groceries and meal kits, and 2,000 for local businesses. Parcel carriers make by far the most deliveries but need the fewest bikes per delivery, because one parcel bike makes 80 drops a day; local businesses make the fewest deliveries but need the most bikes.

math.question: How many electric cargo bikes are working for delivery businesses in London today?
math.expression: parcel_deliveries * parcel_bike_pct / 100 / parcel_per_bike + grocery_deliveries * grocery_bike_pct / 100 / grocery_per_bike + local_deliveries * local_bike_pct / 100 / local_per_bike
math.working: Parcels: 1,200,000 x 10% = 120,000 bike deliveries a day, / 80 per bike = 1,500 bikes. Groceries and meal kits: 300,000 x 15% = 45,000, / 30 = 1,500 bikes. Local businesses: 200,000 x 20% = 40,000, / 20 = 2,000 bikes. Total 5,000 bikes.

math.question: How many new electric cargo bikes will London delivery businesses buy next year?
math.working: Replacements: 5,000 bikes / 4-year life = 1,250 a year. Growth: 25% of 5,000 = 1,250 extra bikes. Total 2,500 new bikes.

math.question: What is the market worth next year, in £ million?
math.working: 2,500 bikes x £6,000 = £15,000,000, which is £15 million a year.

math.question: If Tandrel wins 20% of the market, how much would it sell in London a year, in £ million?
math.working: 20% of £15 million is £3 million a year, above Tandrel's £2 million bar.

brainstorm.question: What could make this market bigger or smaller than your estimate over the next few years?
idea_bank: Tighter low-emission or congestion charges that push more businesses out of vans and onto bikes
More micro-hubs (small depots in central areas) that make short bike rounds possible
Cargo-bike parking and loading bays on busy streets, or a lack of them
Electric vans getting cheaper, which removes the emissions reason to switch to bikes
Longer-lasting bikes and batteries, which lower the number of replacements
Theft and insurance costs putting smaller businesses off
Leasing and rental schemes making bikes affordable for small local businesses
A shortage of riders, or rising riders' pay
Growth slowing once the easy central routes have switched, which would cut the growth half of yearly purchases

must_mention: A market of about £15 million a year: about 2,500 new bikes at £6,000, from a working fleet of about 5,000
At a 20% share Tandrel would sell about £3 million a year, above its £2 million bar
Half of next year's purchases come from fleet growth, so the answer depends most on growth continuing
good_signs: Gives a range, for example £12 million to £18 million
Shows the downside: with no fleet growth the market is about £7.5 million and Tandrel's sales about £1.5 million, below the bar
Suggests how to check the numbers, such as asking large parcel carriers about their bike plans

model_answer_outline: Clarify: next year's spending on new electric cargo bikes by London delivery businesses, valued at the price paid, with leased bikes counted once and takeaway riders' own bikes left out. Tandrel needs £2 million of yearly sales to open a centre.
Structure: working fleet by segment, then yearly purchases (replacements plus growth), then value, then Tandrel's share against its bar.

Fleet: parcels 1,200,000 deliveries a day x 10% by bike / 80 per bike = 1,500; groceries and meal kits 300,000 x 15% / 30 = 1,500; local businesses 200,000 x 20% / 20 = 2,000. About 5,000 bikes in total.
Purchases: 5,000 / 4-year life = 1,250 replacements, plus 25% growth = 1,250 extra bikes. About 2,500 bikes a year.
Value: 2,500 x £6,000 = about £15 million a year. At a 20% share Tandrel would sell about £3 million.
Sense-check and risk: half the purchases come from growth. With no growth the market halves to £7.5 million and Tandrel would sell about £1.5 million, below its bar.
Recommendation: the market is big enough, so open the centre, but start small (for example a service point shared with a partner) and expand once the large parcel carriers confirm their fleet plans.
